Some houses are built for arrival.
Garran Hill was built for return.

The brick gateposts and circular drive establish the scale of the estate with old-world confidence. Arrival here feels less like parking and more like being received.

A House of Proportion, Patina, and Presence

Garran Hill does not announce itself with excess.
Its power is quieter than that.

The estate's grace lies in proportion -- in the measured rhythm of its rooms, in the permanence of brick and timber, in the architectural details that time has deepened rather than diminished.

Flemish bond brick. A water table at the base. White portico. Paired chimneys. Ordered windows. The craftsmanship is not ornamental. It is authorship -- the trace of a hand that understood proportion, patience, and permanence.

Carved mantels, original brass, restored oak, and the kind of room-to-room procession that belongs to another age all contribute to a house that feels composed rather than decorated.

II The Page Provenance

1855 -- 1918

Accession H.1924.7.1

Philip de László · NC Museum of History

Walter Hines Page · 1855 -- 1918

Appointed by Wilson.
He held the alliance from London.

Before Garran Hill was an estate, it was an intention.

Walter Hines Page -- born in Cary, North Carolina. Editor of The Atlantic Monthly. Co-founder of Doubleday, Page & Company. Appointed by Woodrow Wilson as Ambassador to the Court of St. James in 1913 -- and kept there through the years the world came apart.

From London, he commissioned a Moore County country estate. He hired a Boston firm to draw the plans. He sent his son Ralph to supervise the build. Leonard Tufts' own craftsmen -- the same men building Pinehurst two miles away -- laid the brick.

He named it Garran Hill. He never spent a night here.

"Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game." Walter Hines Page · Letter from London · 1915
"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?" Aberdeen station · December 1918
"The friend of Britain in her sorest need." Westminster Abbey · Inscribed 1921

He is the only American diplomat of the first World War honored with a tablet at Westminster Abbey.

Full Brick · Flemish Bond · Neo-Georgian

Built by Leonard Tufts' own craftsmen --
the same men who built Pinehurst.

The house begins in brick -- red, handmade, full-bodied, and laid with the measured rhythm of Flemish bond. The authority is in the masonry. Even the brick pattern feels authored: a house built not for fashion, but for endurance.

III The Rooms

—

The Staircase · 1916

The same curve since 1916.

The mahogany volute turns from the foyer in a single continuous arc -- black railing, wooden treads, the wallpaper rising beside it. It has not been replaced. It has not been rebuilt. The stair still gives the entry its first gesture of grace.

01

The Drawing Room

They made it bigger so they could dance.

Georgian carved mantel. Delft tile surround -- blue and white, hand-painted, original. The coffered ceiling was enlarged for dancing. The Drawing Room is smaller than the Salon by design: it was always meant to be the room you retreat to.

Fire going. No one home yet.

02

The Dining Room · 17 × 19 ft

The original frontispiece. A disappearing folding screen that still works.

The shell cabinets flanking the fireplace are original to the house. The folding screen between the dining room and the hall folds flat and disappears into the wall. It has been doing that since 1916. The windows face east. Morning light comes in low and direct.

03

The Library

Not original. That is the point.

Three walls. Floor to ceiling. The rolling ladder runs the full width. The French doors open to the grounds. In the afternoon, the light through those doors crosses the floor and reaches the spines on the opposite wall.

Dead center of the first floor. Positioned that way in the 2000 plans. When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

04

The Kitchen · 2000 Restoration

The kitchen is not original to 1916.
It is original to the restoration.

Heart-pine floors -- not the oak of the original rooms. White cabinetry. Dark granite. Island. Four windows facing the grounds. O'Shea's drawings document the cabinetry at full scale: Sheet 12. Every cabinet elevation drawn before it was built.

The architectural plans, all 15 sheets, transfer with the property.

05

The Butler's Pantry

The passage between rooms has its own architecture.

Farmhouse sink. Glass-fronted cabinetry. Toile. The butler's pantry extends the kitchen into the old house. A working house built to be used.

06

The Powder Room

A room this small should not work this hard. It does.

Fuchsia chinoiserie wallpaper. Tennessee marble. Ornate brass. Everything in this room was chosen to contrast with the scale of the house around it. It is small on purpose. The detail is the point.

Even the smallest rooms carry ceremony.

07

The Primary Suite

Four bedrooms. Each one with a fireplace.

Custom wall paneling. A fireplace. Drawn for private life. The primary suite has custom wall paneling documented in the restoration drawings. The private floor was treated with the same architectural discipline as the social rooms below.

08

The Mirror Bath

Fuchsia chinoiserie. Tennessee marble.

Gold chandelier. Built-in tub under windows. The grounds visible through every opening. A bath designed for the kind of morning that belongs to this house.

IV The Grounds

4.15 Acres · Pinehurst, NC

The world outside these gates does not exist here.

4.15 acres. The house is only the beginning. Brick-walled saltwater pool, two regulation tennis courts, mature gardens, brick terrace, balcony, and grounds designed for gathering.

The Pool · Salt Water

Twenty by forty feet. The gate opens onto it directly.

Through old iron gates, the 20×40 pool catches afternoon light inside its brick walls. Converted to saltwater in 2022. The brick enclosure dates to the original build.

The Tennis Courts · Private

Two regulation courts. The infrastructure is right.

Two regulation tennis courts with commercial-grade fencing and professional lighting. Night play capable. The surfaces await renewal -- the infrastructure does not.

V The Hollycrest Years

A Private History · 1959 -- 1984

If Walter Hines Page gave the estate its origin, Betty Dumaine gave it its legend.

In 1959, Elizabeth "Betty" Dumaine purchased the property and renamed it Hollycrest, for the native holly trees near the front of the home. She brought horses to the grounds -- thoroughbreds, hunters, a life organized around animals and land.

She kept this land for twenty-five years. One horse she buried here.

Someone still puts flowers there.

MY IRISH HUNTER  ·  BLUE FOX  ·  1946--1965

VI Preserved, Restored, Remembered

The Restoration · 1999 -- 2001

Garran Hill carries the rarest kind of restoration: one that renewed the house without taking away its memory.

Not renovated into anonymity. Restored back into itself. The restoration brought the home into modern life -- new plumbing, electrical, structural work, climate control, custom Marvin windows, security. Yet the soul remained intact.

During restoration, matching the original brick became an act of devotion. The search took three months -- because at Garran Hill, even repair had to respect the original hand.
